items.prompt: Jordan reads code that caps retries at 3, sees nothing explaining why, and assumes it's an arbitrary default. What made that a reasonable assumption to make?
choices: Jordan should have recognized that a round number like 3 is rarely arbitrary and read intent into it anyway
Nothing in the code, docs, or PR history gave any signal the number was a deliberate, load-bearing decision
Jordan should have proactively tracked down whichever engineer attended the meeting eight months ago before touching the code
Retry counts are low-stakes implementation details that are always safe to change without any further research
items.explanation: Jordan acted in good faith on the only evidence available: the code itself, which gave zero indication that '3' was anything other than an untuned default. The failure isn't Jordan's reading comprehension — it's that the decision left no trace anywhere a reasonable person would look before changing it.
items.reference:
Tribal knowledge

Lives in one person's head

ADR

Lives in a searchable, permanent record

Why: a decision only survives the person who made it if it's written somewhere else too.

items.prompt: A decision was made in a meeting eight months ago and never written down. What specifically makes this 'tribal knowledge' rather than just 'a decision that happened'?
choices: The decision itself turned out to be the wrong call, regardless of where it was written down
It exists only as a memory held by whoever was in the room, invisible to anyone who joined later or wasn't there
It was made under time pressure in a single short meeting instead of through a longer formal process
Meetings are inherently unreliable places to make any decision that matters to the team
items.explanation: Tribal knowledge isn't defined by whether a decision was good or bad — it's defined by where it lives. A decision that only exists in people's memories is invisible to anyone who wasn't present, and it disappears entirely the moment everyone who remembers it leaves or forgets.
items.reference:
Tribal knowledge

Lives in one person's head

ADR

Lives in a searchable, permanent record

Why: a decision only survives the person who made it if it's written somewhere else too.

items.prompt: Why is tribal knowledge described as a liability rather than just an inconvenience?
choices: Because it costs nothing until the one person holding it becomes unreachable, at which point the cost can be a real incident
Because relying on memory instead of records always produces the wrong technical decision
Because it means the team is holding far too many meetings to make routine decisions
Because new hires are too intimidated to ever ask questions about undocumented decisions
items.explanation: The cost of tribal knowledge is deferred, not absent — it's invisible right up until the person who holds it leaves, is on leave, or simply isn't asked in time, and then the team pays for it all at once, as Jordan's near-miss shows.
items.reference:
Tribal knowledge

Lives in one person's head

ADR

Lives in a searchable, permanent record

Why: a decision only survives the person who made it if it's written somewhere else too.

items.prompt: What does an ADR capture that a bare code comment like '// retries capped for safety' does not?
choices: Nothing of substance — a short comment conveys exactly the same reasoning, just more concisely
The alternatives that were considered and rejected, and the consequences of the choice — not just the fact that a constraint exists
A record of exactly which engineer is personally responsible for the constraint
A precise reference to the exact line number where the constant is defined
items.explanation: A comment can flag that a number is deliberate, but it rarely has room for why the alternatives lost or what the decision costs going forward. An ADR is built specifically to hold that fuller picture, and it's the fuller picture that would have told Jordan why raising the number was unsafe, not just that it was capped on purpose.
items.reference:
An ADR records:

  • What was decided
  • Why (context + alternatives)
  • What it costs (consequences)

Why: a decision without its reasoning is just an instruction nobody can safely revisit.

items.prompt: A teammate says, 'we already have a wiki, isn't that the same as writing ADRs?' What's the flaw in that framing?
choices: Wikis and ADRs serve the exact same purpose and can always be used interchangeably

A wiki page nobody maintains can go stale and actively mislead readers, while an ADR is a fixed record of one decision at the time it was made and doesn't get silently rewritten to look permanently current
Wikis are strictly better than ADRs since they're easier for anyone to edit at any time
ADRs are a practice that only makes sense for open-source projects with external contributors
items.explanation: The difference isn't the software, it's the discipline: a general wiki page tends to get edited in place to reflect 'current understanding,' which erodes the historical record. An ADR is scoped to one decision and stays as a dated record — when the decision changes, a new ADR supersedes it instead of quietly rewriting history.
items.reference:
An ADR records:

  • What was decided
  • Why (context + alternatives)
  • What it costs (consequences)

Why: a decision without its reasoning is just an instruction nobody can safely revisit.

items.prompt: Why would an ADR have helped Jordan's reviewer catch the problem faster than the review conversation actually did?
choices: It wouldn't have helped — a careful reviewer would always catch this regardless of documentation
A linked ADR would let the reviewer point to a specific, written reason instead of relying on personally remembering an 8-month-old meeting
ADRs are wired into CI so they automatically block any risky pull request from merging
ADRs are thorough enough that they replace the need for code review entirely
items.explanation: The reviewer in L1 caught the issue because they happened to remember the constraint — a fragile, person-dependent safety net. With an ADR linked from the code, that same catch wouldn't depend on the right person happening to be in the review; the reasoning would be sitting right there in writing for anyone to check.
items.reference:
An ADR records:

  • What was decided
  • Why (context + alternatives)
  • What it costs (consequences)

Why: a decision without its reasoning is just an instruction nobody can safely revisit.

items.prompt: Of a meeting with no notes, a Slack thread, and an ADR, which is most findable by someone who joins the team a year later and doesn't know the decision exists?
choices: The meeting, since at least one attendee is bound to remember the reasoning later
The Slack thread, since its content is fully searchable text within the workspace
The ADR, since it's indexed by decision rather than by channel or memory
None of them — a year is long enough that all three become equally unfindable
items.explanation: A Slack thread is technically searchable, but only if the new hire already knows the right keywords to search for — and a meeting with no notes leaves no trace at all. An ADR is deliberately indexed by decision, which is exactly the axis a future reader is searching on ('why does this work this way'), not by channel, date, or who was in the room.
items.reference:
FormatFindable later?
Meeting, no notesNo
Slack threadBarely
ADRYes

items.prompt: Why does a Slack thread only 'barely' count as documentation, even though it's technically searchable?
choices: Slack messages are automatically deleted the moment the conversation goes quiet
It only helps a reader who already knows to search for it, may fall outside the workspace's retention window, and rarely separates the final decision from the back-and-forth that led to it
Slack's search feature doesn't actually index message content at all
Threads inevitably drift completely off-topic before reaching a conclusion
items.explanation: Searchability isn't the same as findability. A reader has to know a relevant thread exists before they can search for it, retention limits can remove it entirely, and even a found thread mixes the decision in with debate, false starts, and tangents — none of which a dedicated ADR has to deal with.
items.reference:

items.prompt: The L1 chart shows 'ask around' costing roughly 180 minutes to a confident answer, versus 5 minutes for 'read the ADR.' What does that gap actually represent?
choices: The chart is measuring how socially comfortable new hires feel asking around
The same underlying question ('why is this the way it is') answered at very different costs depending on where the reasoning was recorded, if anywhere
How long it generally takes to write and ship a piece of code
How many people are currently working on the team at any given time
items.explanation: Both paths answer the exact same question. The gap isn't about the question's difficulty — it's entirely about whether the answer was written somewhere indexed and findable, or has to be reconstructed by asking around and hoping someone still remembers.
items.reference:
Path taken → minutes to a confident answer

Ask around: ~180 · Search Slack: ~90 · Git archaeology: ~45 · Read the ADR: ~5

Why: same question, wildly different cost depending on where the answer was left.

items.prompt: Why does undocumented tribal knowledge cost a new hire specifically more than it costs an existing team member?
choices: It doesn't really differ — every team member pays roughly the same cost regardless of tenure
A new hire doesn't yet know who to ask or what the informal shortcuts are, so they pay the full 'ask around' cost that an existing member might shortcut through familiarity
New hires are generally less capable engineers than people already on the team
Existing team members always write things down the moment they make a decision
items.explanation: An existing team member might get lucky and remember, or know exactly which colleague to ping. A new hire has neither — they're paying the slowest path (asking around, or worse, guessing) by default, precisely when they have the least context to sanity-check a wrong guess.
items.reference:
Path taken → minutes to a confident answer

Ask around: ~180 · Search Slack: ~90 · Git archaeology: ~45 · Read the ADR: ~5

Why: same question, wildly different cost depending on where the answer was left.

items.prompt: If Jordan's team had linked ADR-011 from the retry code from the start, roughly which point on the L1 chart would Jordan's actual experience have landed closest to?
choices: 'Ask around,' since new hires default to asking a colleague before reading anything
'Read the ADR,' since the reasoning would already be sitting next to the code Jordan was reading
'Search Slack,' since Slack is always the default first place anyone looks for context
None of the points — new hires never read any linked documentation at all
items.explanation: The whole point of linking the ADR from the code is to put the cheapest path exactly where the reader already is. Jordan was already looking at the retry constants — a comment pointing to the ADR would have resolved the question in the time it takes to open one linked document, not in the time it takes to track down a person.
items.reference:
Path taken → minutes to a confident answer

Ask around: ~180 · Search Slack: ~90 · Git archaeology: ~45 · Read the ADR: ~5

Why: same question, wildly different cost depending on where the answer was left.

items.prompt: Does 'documentation culture' mean writing an ADR for every decision the team makes, including trivial ones?
choices: Yes — writing an ADR for every decision, however small, is always better regardless of the stakes
No — it means writing down decisions that would be expensive to get wrong twice, in a place future readers will find, not documenting everything indiscriminately
No — ADRs should only ever be written for decisions involving databases or infrastructure
Yes, but only when the decision was made by a senior engineer on the team
items.explanation: The retry cap deserved an ADR because getting it wrong again (or reversing it without knowing why) risks a repeat incident. A variable rename doesn't carry that risk — writing an ADR for it wouldn't add safety, it would just add noise that makes the decisions that do matter harder to find.
items.reference:
Worth an ADR: expensive to reverse, non-obvious reasoning

Not worth one: cheap, reversible, obvious from the code itself

items.prompt: Why would writing an ADR for every small, easily reversible choice actually work against the goal documentation culture is trying to achieve?
choices: It wouldn't — having more recorded decisions is always strictly better for the team
It would bury the decisions that genuinely matter under a pile of low-stakes ones, making the whole ADR index less trustworthy and less likely to be read
ADRs can only be written and approved by tech leads on the team
It would slow down the build pipeline by adding extra required files
items.explanation: Findability is the entire value proposition of an ADR. An index cluttered with trivial entries costs a reader time on every search and trains the team to stop checking it — which quietly recreates the exact tribal-knowledge problem the practice was meant to fix, just with extra paperwork.
items.reference:
Worth an ADR: expensive to reverse, non-obvious reasoning

Not worth one: cheap, reversible, obvious from the code itself

items.prompt: An ADR is marked 'Proposed.' What does that status tell a reader who finds it while working on related code?
choices: This is definitely settled and exactly how the system behaves today
This is still under discussion — the described behavior may not reflect what the system actually does yet
The decision was already rejected and the described approach was abandoned
The document is already out of date and can safely be ignored by readers
items.explanation: 'Proposed' is a deliberate signal that the document describes a draft, not settled reality. A reader who mistakes a proposed ADR for an accepted one risks building on a decision the team hasn't actually committed to.
items.reference:
Proposed → under discussion

Accepted → current, load-bearing

Rejected → kept, not deleted

Superseded → replaced by a newer ADR

items.prompt: Why does the lifecycle keep rejected ADRs in the record instead of deleting them once a proposal is turned down?
choices: Deleting files from the repository is technically difficult to do cleanly
A recorded rejection saves the next person from re-proposing and re-debating the same idea without new information
Keeping rejected ADRs around is a formal legal requirement for the team
It has no real purpose beyond keeping the documentation folder tidy
items.explanation: 'We considered this and said no, here's why' is genuinely useful information on its own — it's the exact thing that lets a future engineer skip re-deriving a debate the team already had, unless they're bringing new evidence that would actually change the answer.
items.reference:
Proposed → under discussion

Accepted → current, load-bearing

Rejected → kept, not deleted

Superseded → replaced by a newer ADR

items.prompt: A decision that was accepted a year ago is revisited and the team decides something materially different. According to the lifecycle, what should happen to the original ADR?
choices: It gets edited in place so it directly describes the new, current decision
It gets marked superseded, and a new ADR is written that links back to it
It gets deleted since it no longer accurately describes current behavior
Nothing — the original ADR stays accepted forever regardless of later changes
items.explanation: The lifecycle treats a changed decision as a new event, not a correction to history. Marking the old ADR superseded and writing a new one preserves both the fact that the original decision was once genuinely in effect and the fact that it's no longer current.
items.reference:
Proposed → under discussion

Accepted → current, load-bearing

Rejected → kept, not deleted

Superseded → replaced by a newer ADR

items.prompt: An ADR states the decision clearly but has no 'Consequences' section. What is a future reader most likely to get wrong as a result?
choices: They'll assume the decision was made unilaterally by a single engineer
They'll assume the decision was free, and be surprised later by a cost or constraint it actually carries
They'll assume the decision is still proposed, not accepted
They'll be unable to find the document in the team's index at all
items.explanation: Every real decision trades something away. Without a stated consequence, a reader has no way to know what that trade-off is — they'll treat the decision as costless right up until they run into the cost it never mentioned, which is exactly what nearly happened with Jordan's retry PR.
items.reference:
SectionAnswers
ContextWhat forced this
DecisionWhat was chosen
AlternativesWhat lost, and why
ConsequencesWhat it costs going forward

items.prompt: Why does the 'Alternatives' section matter even when the author is confident about their recommended option?
choices: It doesn't matter much — alternatives are mostly optional padding text
It lets a reviewer independently judge the reasoning instead of just reacting to the conclusion, and it prevents a rejected idea from being silently re-proposed later
It's only required for ADRs about database or infrastructure decisions
It exists mainly to make the final document look more thorough
items.explanation: Listing what was seriously considered and why it lost gives a reader something to actually evaluate, not just accept on faith. It also means a later engineer who has the same idea can check whether it was already tried and rejected, rather than reopening a settled debate from zero.
items.reference:
SectionAnswers
ContextWhat forced this
DecisionWhat was chosen
AlternativesWhat lost, and why
ConsequencesWhat it costs going forward

items.prompt: An ADR has 'Context' and 'Decision' but skips 'Status + date.' What specifically becomes unclear to a reader?
choices: The underlying reasoning that led to the decision in the first place
Whether the document reflects the system's current behavior or something historical that may have since changed
Who on the team is actually allowed to read the document
Which programming language the decision applies to
items.explanation: Status and date are what let a reader place the document in time. Without them, a five-year-old accepted-then-superseded decision can read exactly like a decision made yesterday, and there's no way to tell the two apart from the text alone.
items.reference:
SectionAnswers
ContextWhat forced this
DecisionWhat was chosen
AlternativesWhat lost, and why
ConsequencesWhat it costs going forward

items.prompt: What's the practical difference between an ADR marked 'Rejected' and one marked 'Superseded'?
choices: There's no meaningful difference — both statuses mean the decision never happened
Rejected means the proposal was never adopted; Superseded means it was adopted and later replaced by a newer decision
Rejected means the proposal was written by a junior, less experienced engineer
Superseded means the original document has been permanently deleted
items.explanation: The two statuses describe different histories. 'Rejected' means the idea never became reality; 'Superseded' means it genuinely was reality for a while before something else replaced it — a distinction that matters if someone is trying to understand how the system actually behaved at a given point in time.
items.reference: A status is a promise about what the document means right now, not what it meant when written.

items.prompt: A reader lands on an ADR marked 'Superseded' with no link to the newer document. What's the actual harm compared to it having that link?
choices: No harm — 'Superseded' already tells the reader everything they need
The reader knows the decision changed but has no path to what it changed to, so they still have to go searching, defeating much of the point of marking it in the first place
The ADR becomes legally invalid and must be deleted immediately
Nothing really changes, since old superseded ADRs are rarely read anyway
items.explanation: Status alone answers 'is this still current,' but a reader who needs the current answer is left stranded without the forward link — they now know they're in the wrong place but not where the right place is, which is only half of the findability an ADR is supposed to provide.
items.reference: A status is a promise about what the document means right now, not what it meant when written.

items.prompt: Why does editing an accepted ADR in place, rather than superseding it, break trust in every other ADR the team has written?
choices: It doesn't — editing is just faster and equally trustworthy, since the content ends up the same either way
If one ADR can be silently rewritten to match current reality, a reader can no longer trust that any ADR reflects what was actually decided at the time it says it was
Editing requires special admin permissions and tooling access that most ordinary engineers don't have
It only affects that one specific document's accuracy, not the trustworthiness of any other ADR
items.explanation: The value of an ADR rests on it being a fixed historical record. Once a reader learns that even one ADR was quietly rewritten after the fact, every other ADR becomes suspect too — there's no longer any way to tell a genuine contemporaneous record from a retroactively tidied-up one.
items.reference:
Edit in place

Erases the trail; looks like the new answer was always true

Supersede

Both versions stay readable and dated

items.prompt: A team switches from polling to webhooks and is deciding whether to edit the old 'use polling' ADR or write a new one. What does superseding preserve that editing would destroy?
choices: Nothing meaningful — the final documented behavior looks identical either way
The fact that polling was ever a deliberate decision at all, along with the original reasoning for it, which helps judge whether a similar future decision should go the same way
The original file's size and formatting exactly as it was first written
The name of whichever engineer happened to write the first version
items.explanation: Superseding keeps both documents intact: one showing polling was chosen for real reasons at the time, and one showing why webhooks replaced it. Editing in place collapses that history into a single document that reads as if webhooks were the answer from day one, hiding the original trade-off entirely.
items.reference:
Edit in place

Erases the trail; looks like the new answer was always true

Supersede

Both versions stay readable and dated

items.prompt: Someone links to an old, now-superseded ADR from a comment written years ago. Why does superseding (rather than deleting the old one) matter for that reader?
choices: It doesn't really matter — old links are generally expected to eventually break
The old link still resolves to a real document, which itself points forward to the current decision, instead of landing on nothing or on rewritten content pretending to be original
Superseded ADRs are automatically removed from the team's search index
It only really matters if the reader happens to be a brand-new hire
items.explanation: A stale link that still resolves to something coherent — even if that something says 'this changed, see the new one' — is far more useful than a dead link or, worse, a link to content silently rewritten to no longer match what it was cited for.
items.reference:
Edit in place

Erases the trail; looks like the new answer was always true

Supersede

Both versions stay readable and dated

items.prompt: An ADR is still marked 'Accepted' a year after the system it describes was quietly changed by an unrelated project. What's the risk of leaving it as-is?
choices: No risk — readers are assumed to treat every old ADR as historical by default
A reader trusts the ADR as current, builds on a description of the system that's no longer true, and has no signal telling them to double-check
The ADR will automatically expire and get archived after one year
Nothing, since ADRs are only read once, right after being written
items.explanation: An ADR's usefulness depends on readers trusting its status. A stale 'Accepted' label doesn't just fail to help — it actively misinforms, because the reader has no reason to suspect the document is out of date unless something explicitly tells them so.
items.reference: A stale record isn't neutral — it actively misleads a reader who trusts it.

items.prompt: What keeps an ADR index useful over time, according to L2's discussion of superseding and status?
choices: Writing as many new ADRs as possible, regardless of how small the decision is
Keeping statuses current — marking things superseded or rejected as reality changes, rather than letting accepted-but-outdated documents accumulate silently
Deleting any ADR that's more than one year old from the index
Only writing ADRs for decisions made by the most senior engineer
items.explanation: Volume isn't the goal — accuracy of status is. An index full of ADRs whose statuses no longer reflect reality is functionally similar to no documentation at all, since a reader can no longer trust any given entry without independently verifying it.
items.reference: A stale record isn't neutral — it actively misleads a reader who trusts it.

items.prompt: ADR-011's Context section describes INC-203 in detail before stating the decision. Why not just state 'retries capped at 3' and skip the incident background?
choices: The incident background is irrelevant padding that just makes the document longer
Without knowing what forced the decision, a reader can't judge whether the cap still applies once the situation that caused it changes
ADRs are required to describe at least one incident
Because Priya personally prefers writing longer, more detailed documents
items.explanation: The Context section is what lets a future reader evaluate the decision instead of just obeying it. If they only see 'capped at 3' with no reason, they can't tell whether that number is still the right one once circumstances change — which is exactly the situation the idempotency-key follow-up work will eventually create.
items.reference:
INC-203: unlimited retries + no idempotency key → 41 double charges

ADR-011: cap at 3, backoff 8s — bounds the overlap window

items.prompt: According to ADR-011, why did unlimited retries cause double charges specifically, rather than just wasted retries?
choices: Because the payment provider's servers were down for an extended maintenance window

Because the client treated a slow-but-successful request as a failure and retried it while the original attempt was still in flight, and there was no idempotency key for the provider to recognize the retry as a duplicate
Because Jordan raised the retry count without review
Because the backoff between retries was not capped at a full 8 seconds
items.explanation: The failure mode was specifically about timing and identity, not just volume: a slow response looked like a failure, triggering a retry, and because nothing told the provider 'this is the same request as before,' both the original and the retry could succeed and both charge the customer.
items.reference:
INC-203: unlimited retries + no idempotency key → 41 double charges

ADR-011: cap at 3, backoff 8s — bounds the overlap window

items.prompt: Priya reconstructed ADR-011's Context from a postmortem that already existed. Why wasn't the postmortem itself sufficient documentation before ADR-011 was written?
choices: Postmortems are generally considered unreliable, untrustworthy sources of information
It was indexed by incident and written for people who lived through it, not connected to the retry code it justified, so nobody reading that code would think to search for it
The postmortem contained factually incorrect information
Postmortems are automatically deleted from the system after 90 days
items.explanation: The information existed, but existing somewhere isn't the same as being documented at the point someone needs it. A postmortem answers 'what happened in this incident'; a reader staring at retry code needs an answer to 'why does this code behave this way,' and nothing connected the two.
items.reference:
INC-203: unlimited retries + no idempotency key → 41 double charges

ADR-011: cap at 3, backoff 8s — bounds the overlap window

items.prompt: ADR-011 names the idempotency-key approach as the actually-correct long-term fix, but the team shipped the retry cap instead. Why record that at all instead of just documenting the cap as the answer?
choices: It shouldn't have been recorded at all — naming a better option undermines the decision made
It gives a future reader a legitimate, documented path to revisit the number once the missing piece exists, instead of either trusting 3 as permanent or overriding it blindly
It's just required boilerplate text in every ADR template the team uses
It makes the document look more thorough for review purposes
items.explanation: Naming the better-but-not-yet-available fix turns the retry cap into an honest 'best answer given current constraints' rather than a claim of permanence. That's what gives a future engineer — including one wanting to eventually raise the cap — a real, sanctioned path forward instead of a guess.
items.reference: Considered: more retries (rejected — caused the incident) · idempotency key (better fix, deferred — needs integration work) · no retries (rejected — turns transient failures into hard failures)

items.prompt: Why was 'no retries at all' rejected as an alternative, according to ADR-011?
choices: Because implementing retries at all turned out to be technically impossible
Because most payment failures are transient and recover on a second attempt, so removing retries would turn common transient failures into hard failures for customers
Because the team had already committed to retries in a different ADR
Because no retries would have been slower than the current approach
items.explanation: The alternative wasn't rejected on implementation grounds — it was rejected because it solves the duplicate-charge problem by creating a worse, more common problem: customers experiencing failures for issues that would have quietly recovered on their own with a retry.
items.reference: Considered: more retries (rejected — caused the incident) · idempotency key (better fix, deferred — needs integration work) · no retries (rejected — turns transient failures into hard failures)

items.prompt: 'Retry more, unchanged otherwise' is listed as a rejected alternative in ADR-011. Why include an option that's essentially what caused the original incident?
choices: To pad out the document's length with an obviously bad, easily dismissed idea
Because it's exactly the option someone unfamiliar with the history (like Jordan) is likely to propose again, so recording why it failed once heads that off
Because the team was genuinely still undecided about pursuing that option
It shouldn't be included; only viable options belong in an ADR
items.explanation: Including the option that already failed is precisely what closes the loop on Jordan's near-miss — it's the option Jordan's PR effectively proposed. Recording it as considered-and-rejected, with the specific reason, is what lets the next person who has the same instinct find the answer before repeating the incident.
items.reference: Considered: more retries (rejected — caused the incident) · idempotency key (better fix, deferred — needs integration work) · no retries (rejected — turns transient failures into hard failures)

items.prompt: ADR-011's Consequences section states that a payment can still fail permanently after 3 attempts. Why does that matter to someone who isn't touching the retry logic at all?
choices: It doesn't — only the retry code's author needs to know this
Any caller of the checkout flow needs to handle a genuine permanent failure explicitly, rather than assuming retries always eventually succeed
It's only relevant to the payment provider, not the engineering team
It means the retry logic is broken and needs to be rewritten
items.explanation: Consequences ripple outward from the decision to anyone building near it. A developer writing the UI that calls checkout needs to know failure is a real, expected outcome after 3 tries — otherwise they'll build a flow that has no path for 'this genuinely didn't work,' assuming retries are a guarantee they aren't.
items.reference: A payment can still fail permanently after 3 tries — callers must handle that, not assume retries always succeed.

items.prompt: What would be missing for a future reader if ADR-011 stated the decision and alternatives but left out the Consequences section entirely?
choices: Nothing important — the Decision and Alternatives sections already cover everything needed

The fact that raising the retry cap again, without first adding the idempotency key, would reintroduce the exact failure from INC-203 — the specific risk of touching this number without the missing piece
A record of the specific engineer who originally wrote the ADR
The exact calendar date on which the decision was originally made
items.explanation: Consequences is where the ADR states the sharp edge explicitly: this number is safe *because* of a missing piece elsewhere, and changing it without that piece recreates the original incident. That's the single fact most directly relevant to preventing a repeat of Jordan's PR.
items.reference: A payment can still fail permanently after 3 tries — callers must handle that, not assume retries always succeed.

items.prompt: A team relies on 'see PR #482 for context' instead of writing a standalone ADR. What specifically makes this fail as documentation?
choices: PR descriptions are technically incapable of containing any real explanatory text
PRs are indexed and searched by code change, not by decision, so nobody trying to answer 'why is this the way it is' would think to search PR history for the reasoning
GitHub automatically deletes PR descriptions after about a year
It works exactly as well as an ADR, just in a different location
items.explanation: The problem isn't that the information is inaccessible in principle — it's that it's filed under the wrong index for how anyone will actually look for it. A future reader searching 'why retries capped at 3' has no natural path to PR #482 unless they already know that PR exists.
items.reference: PRs are indexed by code change. ADRs are indexed by decision. Only one of those is what a future reader is searching by.

items.prompt: Why does 'no link from the code' count as its own separate anti-pattern from 'decision buried in a PR description,' even though both leave a reader stuck?
choices: They're really the same underlying anti-pattern, just described with different names
A written, standalone ADR can still fail to help if nothing at the point of use (the code itself) tells the reader it exists — the ADR being well-written doesn't fix a missing pointer to it
Only PR descriptions can be considered documentation at all
Because code comments are technically not allowed to link elsewhere
items.explanation: A well-written ADR that's never referenced from the code it explains fails for the same practical reason as no ADR at all: the reader standing at the retry constants has no way to know it exists. Writing the record and making it discoverable from where someone will actually be standing are two distinct steps, and both have to happen.
items.reference: PRs are indexed by code change. ADRs are indexed by decision. Only one of those is what a future reader is searching by.

items.prompt: Priya added a comment above `maxRetries: 3` pointing to ADR-011. What specific gap does that comment close that writing the ADR alone didn't?
choices: It fixes an actual latent bug that existed in the retry logic itself
It puts a pointer to the reasoning exactly where a future reader (like Jordan) will already be looking, instead of requiring them to already know the ADR exists
It makes writing the ADR document itself completely unnecessary
It permanently prevents the retry code from ever being changed again
items.explanation: Writing ADR-011 solved 'is this decision recorded anywhere.' The comment solves the separate problem of discoverability — without it, a correct, complete ADR sitting in an index somewhere is no more helpful in practice than the original unwritten decision, because nothing leads a reader to it.
items.reference: PRs are indexed by code change. ADRs are indexed by decision. Only one of those is what a future reader is searching by.

items.prompt: ADR-011 states it 'should be superseded once the idempotency key work lands.' If that work ships, why write a new ADR rather than just updating ADR-011 to say 'retries are now unlimited'?
choices: Because ADR-011 is technically locked in a system that prevents any editing at all

Because editing it in place would erase the record that a 3-retry cap was ever a deliberate, reasoned decision — a future reader would lose the ability to see why the constraint existed and what removed it
Because superseding is required by company policy for all documents
There's no real difference; either approach is equally fine
items.explanation: Superseding keeps ADR-011 intact as evidence that the cap was a real, justified decision at the time, with a clear pointer to what changed. Editing it away would make it look as if unlimited retries were always safe, hiding exactly the reasoning that would matter if a similar constraint ever needs to be added again.
items.reference: ADR-011 will be superseded once the idempotency key ships — not edited to pretend the cap was never needed.

items.prompt: Suppose the idempotency-key work ships but turns out to have its own limitation, and the team wants to reintroduce a retry cap. How does having superseded (rather than edited) ADR-011 help in that future moment?
choices: It doesn't really help — the old, superseded ADR would be irrelevant either way
The original reasoning, alternatives, and consequences from ADR-011 are still intact and readable, giving the team a documented starting point instead of re-deriving the same analysis from scratch
Superseded ADRs are automatically re-applied by the system
It only helps if the exact same engineer is still on the team
items.explanation: A superseded ADR isn't dead weight — it's a preserved analysis the team can reopen. If circumstances swing back toward needing a cap, ADR-011's original Context, Alternatives, and Consequences are still there to build from, which an edited-away version wouldn't offer.
items.reference: ADR-011 will be superseded once the idempotency key ships — not edited to pretend the cap was never needed.

items.prompt: What does ADR-011 marking itself as a candidate for future superseding, right in its own Consequences section, accomplish that a purely retrospective note added later couldn't?
choices: Nothing really — flagging this in advance has no practical effect either way

It tells a reader up front, at the moment they trust the document as current, exactly what condition would make it stop being current — rather than leaving that discovery to whoever eventually stumbles on it
It automatically schedules a calendar reminder for the team
It actually means the ADR itself is not yet accepted as final
items.explanation: Flagging the condition for its own obsolescence inside the document itself means a reader doesn't have to guess whether the decision is still solid — the document tells them exactly what to watch for, turning 'is this still true' from an open question into a specific, checkable one.
items.reference: ADR-011 will be superseded once the idempotency key ships — not edited to pretend the cap was never needed.
